title: The imperative and negation

objectives.can: Recognise Qal imperatives and their gender and number.
Read לֹא, אַל and אֵין and say what kind of sentence each negates.

explanation.summary: The imperative is the form that gives a command. It is made from the yiqtol stem without its prefix, and it exists only in the second person. Hebrew does not put a negative word in front of it: to forbid, it uses a different construction. This lesson also teaches the three small words for 'not' that you will meet most.

sections.heading: The imperative: the yiqtol stem without its prefix
body: The imperative is used when someone is spoken to directly and told to do something: 'listen', 'go', 'say'. It is always second person, so it has no person to name; you only need to give its gender and number. The masculine singular is simply the yiqtol stem with the prefix taken away, as in שְׁמֹר 'keep!' beside the yiqtol יִשְׁמֹר.

The other forms add the same endings as the yiqtol: -וּ for the masculine plural, -ִי for the feminine singular and -נָה for the feminine plural. As in the yiqtol, the stem vowel shortens or goes to a shewa when an ending is added, so the masculine plural of שְׁמַע is שִׁמְעוּ and the feminine singular is שִׁמְעִי.
An imperative may carry a prefixed וְ: 'and go', 'and say'. The conjunction does not change the form.

head: Gender and number
Ending added to the imperative stem

sections.heading: The lengthened imperative and the feminine plural
body: A masculine singular imperative sometimes has an extra ending -ָה. It makes no difference of person or number: it is still a command to one man. The ending often adds a note of urgency or of address, or it is simply a habit of certain verbs. You can see it in שִׁמְעָה beside שְׁמַע, in שִׁכְבָה and in שִׁלְחָה.

The feminine plural is rare, because commands to a group of women are rare. The examples below, from Ruth 1, are among the clearest in the Bible: Naomi tells her two daughters-in-law to go and to return.

sections.heading: Three words for 'not': לֹא, אַל, אֵין
body: לֹא is the ordinary 'not'. It stands before a finite verb and says that something is not, was not or will not be so: 'I did not know', 'they will not cease'. Before a yiqtol it can also say what must not be done as a standing rule or in a general commandment: 'you shall not eat of it', 'you shall not murder'. It can also negate a clause with no verb: 'it is not good'.

אַל is used to forbid something on a particular occasion, to a person who is being addressed: 'do not fear', 'do not stretch out your hand'. It stands before a verb in the jussive, the short form of the yiqtol that expresses a wish or command. In a strong verb the jussive and the yiqtol often look the same, so you may not be able to tell them apart by the verb; the word אַל tells you what kind of sentence you have. The little word נָא, which can follow אַל, makes the request polite or urgent.

אֵין negates a different kind of sentence: it says that something does not exist or is not present, 'there is not' or 'there is no'. It can stand before a noun ('there is no man'), take a pronominal suffix ('he is not', 'it is not here') or stand before a participle to say that someone is not doing something. In this role it takes the place that the verb 'to be' would have in a verbless clause, which is why it belongs with the nominal clauses you met earlier. A variant spelling, אַיִן, is also found.
The word בִּלְתִּי negates an infinitive: 'not to eat', 'so as not to …'.

sections.heading: How to forbid, and how to say 'do not'
body: Biblical Hebrew has no negative imperative. The imperative itself is never negated. To tell someone not to do something, the speaker uses either לֹא with a yiqtol or אַל with a jussive, depending on what kind of prohibition it is.

Grammarians commonly distinguish a prohibition that is a settled law (לֹא) from one that applies to a moment or an act (אַל), and this is a useful rule of thumb. It is a tendency, not an absolute rule: read the verse and decide from what is said. The commandments of Exodus 20 are put with לֹא.

misunderstandings: A command to forbid is not לֹא + imperative. The imperative cannot be negated; use the yiqtol or jussive with לֹא or אַל.
אֵין is not the ordinary 'not'. It says something is absent or does not exist; לֹא negates a verb.
The ending -ָה on a masculine imperative does not make it feminine or plural. The gender and number are those of the bare form.
A form like תִּירָא after אַל does not have to look different from a yiqtol. Both are second masculine singular here; the negative word shows that this is a prohibition.

deeper.heading: Why the imperative has no negative
body: Many languages negate their commands with a special word; Hebrew uses אַל with the short yiqtol for this purpose. Some grammarians explain this as a trace of an older pattern in which the particle אַל took a short form of the verb. This is a historical explanation, not one that a reader needs in order to read the texts.

examples.analysis: לֶךְ is the masculine singular imperative of יָלַךְ 'go': God speaks to Abram. The command is built on a stem with no prefix and no ending. It is followed by לְךָ, a preposition with the suffix of the second person, which gives the command a nuance 'for yourself'. The form begins the whole account of Abram's journey.

examples.analysis: אַל before תִּשְׁלַח and (after וְ) before תַּעַשׂ makes a prohibition, 'do not stretch out … do not do', to Abraham on this one occasion. The verbs are second masculine singular, the same in shape as a yiqtol. The command is not an imperative with a negative: there is no negative imperative.
